column1: What are the four facets of learning a programming language?
column2: Syntax & semantics, paradigm, artifact ecosystem (build/run/packages), and tooling.

Runs the linter — a free expert code review. Follow its suggestions.
Automatically formats your code.

Shadowing creates a NEW binding with the same name (old value hidden). Mutation changes the value in place and requires `let mut`.
`i32` (the default integer). Floats default to `f64`.

column1: In Rust, what is an expression?
column2: A block of code that produces a value. The last expression in a block is its value. `if`, `match`, and `{}` blocks are all expressions.

column1: Why is there no ternary operator in Rust?
column2: Because `if` is an expression — it produces a value directly, so a ternary is unnecessary.
`String` is owned, growable, heap-allocated. `&str` is a borrowed, immutable view (a string slice).
A `&'static str` literal baked into the binary — NOT a `String`. Convert with `.to_string()` or `String::from(...)`.

column1: Does `s.len()` on a String count bytes or characters?
column2: BYTES. Use `s.chars().count()` for characters. `"héllo"` is 6 bytes but 5 chars.

column1: What does `5 / 2` evaluate to in Rust?
column2: `2` — integer division truncates. Use floats (`5.0 / 2.0`) for `2.5`.
A `match` must cover EVERY possible case — the compiler refuses to compile if a case is missing.
(1) Each value has exactly one owner. (2) Only one owner at a time. (3) When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped.

column1: What happens when you pass a `String` to a function?
column2: It MOVES — the function becomes the new owner and the original variable is invalid afterward.
Ownership transfers to the new location; the old binding is dead (using it is a compile error).
(1) Many `&T` OR one `&mut T` — never both at once. (2) References must always be valid (never dangle).
Borrows end at their LAST USE, not at the end of the scope — so a mutable borrow is allowed after a shared borrow is no longer used.
Copy = implicit bit copy (i32, bool, char, tuples of Copy). Clone = explicit `.clone()` (String, Vec). Move = default for non-Copy types; ownership transfers.

column1: Why does passing an `i32` not move it, but a `String` does?
column2: `i32` implements `Copy` (cheap bit copy). `String` owns heap data, so passing it transfers ownership (a move).
A view into a contiguous range of data — a pointer + a length. `&str` slices a String; `&[i32]` slices a Vec.

column1: What does `'a` mean in `fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str`?
column2: A lifetime parameter: the returned reference is valid as long as both inputs are valid.

column1: Why can't a function return a reference to a local variable?
column2: The local is dropped when the function returns, so the reference would dangle. The compiler rejects it.
Resource Acquisition Is Initialization — the owner of a value IS its cleanup. When the owner goes out of scope, resources are freed deterministically. No GC needed.

column1: When is a Rust value freed (vs Python's GC)?
column2: When its owner goes out of scope — deterministic and exactly once. Python's GC frees nondeterministically when it notices the object is unreachable.

column1: struct vs enum — when to use each?
column2: struct = has ALL its fields at once (AND). enum = IS ONE OF several variants (OR).
Auto-implements the Debug trait so the type prints with `{:?}` (programmer-readable).
`&self` borrows immutably; `&mut self` borrows mutably; `self` CONSUMES the value (moves it).
Forgetting a case (or adding a new variant later) is a compile error, not a runtime bug. The compiler walks you through every `match` to update.
Option = maybe a value (None / Some). Result = ok OR error with data (Ok / Err). Option asks "is there a value?"; Result asks "did it succeed and what went wrong?"
`struct UserId(u64);` — wraps a primitive to give it meaning and prevent accidentally mixing types. Compile-time type safety.
Shorthand to match ONE pattern and ignore the rest: `if let Some(v) = opt { ... }`.
Irrefutable always match (`let x = 5`). Refutable can fail (`let Some(v) = opt`). `let` requires irrefutable; refutable needs `if let` / `match` / `let else`.
Only when every field is `Copy` (primitives). Types with String/Vec fields cannot be Copy.

column1: How is Rust's enum different from Java's?
column2: Rust enums can carry data per variant and matches must be exhaustive. Java enums are named constants.
Errors are RETURN VALUES (part of the function's type signature), not thrown. The compiler forces you to handle them.
Unwraps `Ok(x)` or returns early with `Err` (converted via `From`). The enclosing function must return `Result` or `Option`.
Panic = programmer error / broken invariant (unrecoverable). Result = expected, recoverable failure (bad input, missing file, network).

column1: What two traits must a custom error type implement?
column2: `Display` (printable) and `std::error::Error` (first-class error). Also derive `Debug`.
Converts `Option<T>` → `Result<T,E>`: `None` becomes the `Err(e)` you supply.
`map` transforms the success value (T→U). `and_then` chains an operation that itself returns Option/Result.
It documents WHY the unwrap is safe — if it panics, the message tells you which invariant broke.
Via the `From` trait — your error type implements `From<std::io::Error>` (or uses `thiserror`'s `#[from]`), so `?` converts for you.

column1: What does `fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>` allow?
column2: Using `?` in main; errors bubble up and print to stderr with a non-zero exit code.
`iter()` yields `&T` (borrows). `iter_mut()` yields `&mut T`. `into_iter()` yields owned `T` and CONSUMES the collection.

column1: What does `for x in v` do to `v`?
column2: Desugars to `into_iter()` — it CONSUMES v. Use `for x in &v` to borrow instead.
Gathers iterator items into a collection. The target type comes from context (annotation or return type).
Gets or inserts a key's value, returning a mutable reference to it — the idiomatic "count occurrences" pattern.
The compiler generates a specialized copy of generic code for each concrete type — generic Rust is as fast as hand-written code (no boxing or erasure).
map transforms each item; filter keeps items where the predicate is true; fold accumulates with an initial value.
Yes — an iterator chain does nothing until something consumes it (collect, sum, a for loop).
A missing key is an expected case, not a crash. Returning Option forces you to handle absence.
HashMap is unordered but fast. BTreeMap keeps keys SORTED (iterate in order, find ranges).

column1: Translate `[x*x for x in range(10) if x%2==0]` to Rust.
column2: `(0..10).filter(|x| x % 2 == 0).map(|x| x * x).collect()`
A set of methods that types can implement — like a Java interface, but with default methods, associated types, and compile-time generics. Rust has no inheritance.
Generics = monomorphized, zero runtime cost, one concrete type per Vec. dyn = dynamic dispatch via vtable, enables heterogeneous collections.
The rules for using a trait as `dyn Trait`. A trait with generic METHODS is not object-safe.
Fn captures by reference (read-only, many calls). FnMut captures by mutable reference. FnOnce captures by value and can be called once.

column1: What does `move` do in a closure?
column2: Forces capture by value (ownership) instead of borrowing — needed to send closures to another thread.
A trait method with a body — implementors get it for free and can override it.

column1: Why `Box<dyn Plugin>` for a plugin registry?
column2: Heterogeneous collection — different concrete types can't live in one `Vec<T>`. Trait objects erase the concrete type.
Display = human-readable (`{}`), implemented manually. Debug = programmer-readable (`{:?}`), derived.
You can implement a trait for a type only if at least one of them is local to your crate.
A crate is a compilation unit (lib.rs or main.rs). Modules organize code WITHIN a crate.
`pub` makes an item visible outside its module; `pub(crate)` limits visibility to the crate. Privacy is the default.
In the `tests/` directory — they test the PUBLIC API exactly as an external consumer would.
A code block inside a `///` doc comment that `cargo test` compiles and runs — your docs can never rot.

column1: What does `cargo add serde --features derive` do?
column2: Adds serde with the `derive` feature enabled, so you can use `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]`.
A set of related crates in one repo sharing a Cargo.toml, lockfile, and build. Tauri is a workspace of ~10 crates.
`#[test]` marks a test function. `#[should_panic]` marks a test that PASSES if it panics.
Warns on every public item that has no doc comment — a quality bar real crates use.

column1: Unit vs integration tests — which sees private items?
column2: Unit tests (inside `#[cfg(test)] mod tests`) can access private items. Integration tests only the public API.
Box = single owner, heap allocation. Rc = refcounted shared ownership, single-threaded. Arc = atomic Rc, safe across threads.

column1: Why do recursive types need a `Box`?
column2: A recursive type would be infinitely sized. Box adds one pointer of indirection, breaking the recursion.
Moves the borrow check to RUNTIME — `borrow()`/`borrow_mut()` panic on violation. For interior mutability (shared mutable data). Single-threaded.
Code run when a value goes out of scope — RAII cleanup (File closes, MutexGuard unlocks, Box frees).

column1: Why does `fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str` need no explicit lifetime?
column2: Lifetime elision: with exactly one input reference, its lifetime is assigned to the output.
A reference that lives for the entire program (string literals are `&'static str`).

column1: Why is `Option<&T>` the same size as `&T`?
column2: Niche optimization — a `&T` is never null, so the null pointer is used as the `None` tag. Free Option.
`u8` has no niche — all 256 bit patterns are valid values, so a separate tag byte is needed.
Guarantees a C-compatible memory layout (field order + alignment) — needed for FFI.
Struct fields drop in declaration order; variables in a scope drop in reverse declaration order (LIFO).
Send = safe to move to another thread. Sync = safe to share by reference across threads. Both are compiler-enforced.
Its reference count is not atomic — concurrent updates would race. `Rc` is `!Send`.
Channels pass OWNERSHIP of data (pipelines, decoupled stages). Mutex SHARES mutable data among threads.
Suspends the current task, freeing the thread for other work, and resumes when the future completes. Non-blocking.
Threads = OS threads, real parallelism, for CPU-bound work. Tasks = lightweight, multiplexed, for I/O-bound work, thousands at once.
Sets up the tokio runtime and runs your async main on it. Without a runtime, futures never run.
tokio::spawn creates a lightweight TASK on the runtime; thread::spawn creates an OS thread.
Waits on multiple futures and runs the code for whichever completes first (like Promise.race).

column1: Why does Rust guarantee no data races?
column2: The type system enforces Send/Sync at compile time — a data race is unrepresentable.

column1: What are the four powers of `unsafe`?
column2: (1) Dereference raw pointers. (2) Call unsafe functions / FFI. (3) Access or mutate mutable statics. (4) Implement unsafe traits (Send/Sync).
No — it only grants the four powers. All safe rules still apply inside an unsafe block.

column1: Why is dereferencing a raw pointer unsafe?
column2: The pointer could be null, dangling, misaligned, or aliased — the compiler can't verify the invariants.
CString = owned, NUL-terminated (built with `CString::new`, errors on embedded NUL). CStr = borrowed view into a C string.
Prevents symbol name mangling so C can link to the function by its plain name.
A C-compatible dynamic library (.so / .dll / .dylib) linkable from C, Python ctypes, or any FFI-capable language.
Confine all `unsafe` to small, reviewed functions that expose a SAFE API — callers never touch unsafe.

column1: Who frees memory returned from an extern "C" function?
column2: Depends on the function's documented contract (caller or callee). Document the ownership in the wrapper's SAFETY comment.
Exact C-compatible layout (field order + alignment) — a stable ABI contract for FFI.

column1: Order Tauri's stack from top to bottom.
column2: tauri → tauri-runtime → tauri-runtime-wry → wry (webview) → tao (windowing).
Turns a Rust function into one callable from the frontend via invoke — generates the IPC plumbing.
Async commands run on tokio (for slow I/O, keeps the UI responsive). Sync commands run on the main thread (fast work).

column1: How do you share state with Tauri commands?
column2: Register with `app.manage(MyState)`, then inject with `state: State<'_, MyState>`.

column1: The three jobs of a Tauri plugin?
column2: (1) Rust functionality. (2) Glue/hooks to integrate into an app. (3) A JavaScript API for the frontend.
Security — they declare which commands the frontend may invoke, limiting blast radius.

column1: Where does most `unsafe` live in Tauri?
column2: In wry and tao — they talk to the OS webview/windowing C APIs directly.

column1: What's the first thing to read in an unfamiliar codebase?
column2: README, then ARCHITECTURE.md, then the tests, then trace one feature end-to-end from its entry point.
A small, well-scoped, maintainer-curated issue for newcomers — low risk and teaches the contribution workflow.

column1: Why split a core library from a Tauri app?
column2: Testability (pure `cargo test`, no windowing system) and decoupling (portable core, thin app layer).
Commands run on tokio's multi-threaded runtime, so state needs thread-safe interior mutability. RefCell is `!Sync`.

column1: Why return `Result<Note, String>` from a command?
column2: String serializes cleanly to the frontend. Tradeoff: the frontend loses structured error info (use an enum if it must branch on error type).

column1: Why is the `Store` not wrapped in `Arc`?
column2: There's exactly one owner (the app), shared via State + Mutex. Arc is only needed for multiple independent owners.

column1: Safest way to add FFI to an app?
column2: Confine it to one small module using the safe-wrapper pattern, with a documented `// SAFETY:` comment.
